subject: Coffee & Tea
title: What Is Green Coffee?
description: A quick win: understand What Is Green Coffee?.

hook.text: Before roasting, coffee beans are pale green, smell like grass, and taste like nothing you'd recognize as coffee.

buildup.text: Green beans are the dried seeds inside a coffee cherry. They're dense, hard, and stable for months in storage.

discovery.text: All the flavor you associate with coffee—chocolate, caramel, fruit, nuttiness—doesn't exist yet. Heat creates it.

twist.text: Green coffee has been traded for centuries as a commodity. Only in the last 150 years has roasting become a separate craft.

climax.text: The transformation from green seed to aromatic brown bean is one of the most complex chemical reactions in food science.

punchline.text: No heat, no coffee. Everything you taste was created by roasting.

quiz.question: What does green coffee taste like before roasting?

details.summary: Green coffee is the raw, unroasted seed inside the coffee cherry. It has a grassy smell, a pale green color, and virtually none of the flavors we associate with brewed coffee. Roasting transforms it through hundreds of chemical reactions.
details.whyItMatters: Every cup of coffee begins as green coffee, so understanding this starting material explains why origin, variety, and processing influence the final taste.
takeaways: Green coffee is the unroasted seed of the coffee cherry
It contains over 1,000 compounds that change during roasting
Quality at the green stage sets the ceiling for the roasted cup

faq.question: How long can green coffee beans be stored before quality degrades?
faq.answer: Green coffee typically stays fresh for six to twelve months when stored in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After that, the beans gradually lose moisture and flavor potential, a process called past-crop aging.

faq.question: Why does green coffee smell grassy instead of like brewed coffee?
faq.answer: The aromatic compounds we recognize as coffee flavor only form during the Maillard reaction and caramelization that occur at high roasting temperatures. Without heat, the raw bean retains its vegetal, hay-like scent.
